concept.body: Cavalieri as a comparison engine: align two solids of the same height; if every level's cross-section areas are EQUAL the volumes are equal, and if one solid's sections are always k times the other's, its volume is k times as large. This prices oblique cones (⅓πr²h with vertical height) and curvy solids with known constant sections.

explanationVariants: Every section is 3 times as large, same height.

widget.prompt: Solid B's every cross-section is triple solid A's (same heights). A's volume is 20. B's = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 20 copies A — triple slices at every level: 60.

steps.body: Cavalieri also compares UNLIKE solids. Chapter 1 found the circle-in-square section ratio: π/4 at every height. Promote it: if one solid's sections are always k times another's (same height), its volume is k times as large — the equal-slices principle, run through a constant multiplier.

explanationVariants: The prism: 6 × 6 × 10 = 360. The inscribed cylinder's sections are π/4 of the squares at every level.

widget.prompt: A square prism (side 6, height 10) circumscribes a cylinder (radius 3, height 10). The cylinder's volume (2 decimals) = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 360 is the PRISM — the cylinder claims the π/4 share of every slice: 90π ≈ 282.74.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Section ratio π/4 at every height ⇒ volume ratio π/4: (π/4)(360) = 90π ≈ 282.74.

explanationVariants: A leaning cone's sections match its upright twin's at every level — similarity shrinks both alike.

widget.prompt: A leaning (oblique) cone: base radius 6, vertical height 10. Volume coefficient (of π) = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 360 skips the ⅓ — cones (upright or leaning) claim a third: 120.
200 uses r = √60-ish — ⅓(6²)(10) = 120, lean or no lean.

widget.fallbackFeedback: ⅓π(36)(10) = 120π — Cavalieri extends the ⅓ to oblique cones for free.

steps.body: The comparison move generalizes beautifully: any solid squeezed slice-for-slice between two others inherits their verdicts, and any solid whose sections COPY a known solid's (however the stacking bends) copies its volume. Next chapter this becomes an engine: the sphere's volume will fall out of a cylinder-minus-cone comparison, slice by slice.

explanationVariants: To use Cavalieri you need same heights and a slice-area relationship at every level.
Matching the pair level-for-level is the whole method.

widget.prompt: To prove two solids have equal volume via Cavalieri, you must establish:

options.label: Same height, and equal cross-section areas at every single level
options.feedback: Both clauses carry weight — the height aligns the slicing, and 'every level' seals it.

options.label: Equal surface areas
options.feedback: Surface area is a different (and shear-fragile) quantity — Cavalieri trades only in slice areas.

options.label: Equal bases and equal tops
options.feedback: Ends matching says nothing about the middle — EVERY level must match.

options.label: That both are solids of revolution
options.feedback: The principle is shape-agnostic — prisms, deformed stacks, anything sliceable qualifies.

predict.prompt: Every cross-section of solid B has exactly half the area of A's at the same height. What is B's volume?

options.label: Half of A's — the ratio carries straight through
A quarter — areas scale as the square

predict.reveal: Half. Volume is the accumulation of slices, so a constant ratio between the slices passes straight to the total — no squaring, because nothing is being scaled in two directions here. Sweep and watch the ratio hold at every height.

widget.prompt: Sweep the plane and check the two area readouts at several matching heights. Does their RATIO ever change?
widget.successFeedback: The ratio held at every height you tested — so it holds for the accumulated total too. A constant slice ratio is a volume ratio; that is Cavalieri used as a scale, not just as an equality.
widget.positionFeedback: Keep sweeping, then settle at the middle height to finish the reading.
widget.comparisonFeedback: Add the second solid — a ratio needs two readouts, and there is only one on screen.
widget.invariantFeedback: Test more heights first. 'Every cross-section' is a claim about all of them, and it is the constancy you are checking.

widget.prompt: A rectangular prism is 'bent' into a gentle S-curve — every cross-section perpendicular to the original height stays the same rectangle, at the same levels. Its volume:

options.label: Unchanged — Cavalieri doesn't care HOW the slices are stacked, only what they are at each level
options.feedback: Straight, sheared, or S-curved: the stacking path is free. (Real bending often distorts sections — the stated hypothesis is what licenses the verdict.)

options.label: Less — curves compress
options.feedback: If sections truly stay congruent at each level (as stated), the volume is level-by-level identical.

options.label: More — the S is longer
options.feedback: Arc-length grows, but volume reads the slices — unchanged.

options.label: Cavalieri can't apply to curved stacks
options.feedback: The principle is exactly about ignoring the stacking — slices rule.

hints: Check Cavalieri's hypothesis: the vase's stated section areas vs the cylinder's, level by level.
The cylinder's sections are constantly π(5²) = 25π.
The vase: 25π at every level too (its BOUNDARY curves, but the given areas hold) — conclude, then compute πr²h.
explanationVariants: Both solids present 25π at every one of the 12 levels of height: equal volumes. V = π(25)(12) = 300π.
Equal slices, height 12: the vase costs the cylinder's 300π.

widget.prompt: A curvy vase of height 12 has horizontal cross-section area 25π at EVERY height — the same as a radius-5 cylinder of height 12. The vase's volume coefficient (of π) = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 100 = ⅓(25)(12) applies a cone's third — constant sections mean cylinder pricing: 25 × 12 = 300.
60 = 5 × 12 forgets the square — the section is already 25π: coefficient 25 × 12 = 300.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Constant 25π sections over height 12: V = 300π — curvature of the WALL never entered the bill.

takeaways: Constant section ratio k at every level ⇒ volume ratio k (the π/4 cylinder-in-prism).
Oblique cones inherit the ⅓ for free; curvy solids with known sections price like their straight twins.
The method: align heights, relate sections at every level, conclude.
steps.teaser: Next: what Cavalieri does NOT promise — surface area and the converse.
